scrollSteps.value: Growing up in the 1990s felt like a communal experience. Before the internet became the internet we all shared similar schedules. We remember exactly when we saw Rose and Jack cling to that one damn door in freezing water because we all saw it at the same time. Saturday nights were reserved for All That and weekday afternoons were hosted by Carson Daly. We moved like a giant ball of rumbling prepubescent anxiety.

But when Britney Spears strutted onto TRL in pigtails and a school uniform, some of us felt flung to the outer edges of this homogenous bubble by sapphic yearning. Suddenly our timelines didn’t sync up. Did we want to be her or be with her?
We weren’t sure, but we felt isolated, believing there was no one out there who understood our otherness.
Unbeknownst to us, we inadvertently created shared touchpoints that, as out and proud adults, we still use to connect with one another.

We waited with baited breath for Xena to kiss Gabrielle. We became regular watchers of the nascent WNBA. And we wore out our rented VHSs of Cruel Intentions under the guise that “Ryan Phillippe was hot.” No, it was definitely not that droolworthy Selma Blair and Sarah Michelle Gellar scene. Our connections continued to build, even if we couldn’t see them at the time.
This is the story of one such connection. Meet Ashleé and Jan.

Ashleé grew up knowing she was different, but was unable to put a name on the flutters she felt when certain women popped up on her TV. And as an adult, the bounds of compulsory heterosexuality sucked out the space for her to imagine life as gay woman. Jan was closeted in high school because she was still figuring out her sexuality and was terrified of the negative impact that coming out would have on the people she respected.

We connected in college hiding in plain sight. As staff members on Western Kentucky University’s student newspaper, we spent several semesters together, hovering over beige Macs as we edited and designed two issues a week. When we met, neither of us had fully acknowledged our queerness. We were both dating men.

By the time we reconnected in our 30s, Jan was out and married to a woman. Ashleé was divorced from a man and identified as queer. Yet as our paths to discovering and nurturing our queerness diverged, we could still point to the same pivotal moments in popular culture that served as breadcrumbs to our own self discoveries.

timelineInstructions.value: Each side of this timeline represents a personal journey: Jan’s on the left and Ashleé’s on the right.

The rainbow lines represent overarching themes, and the dots are events within those themes. You can use the rainbow dots at the top to be reminded of the full theme definition anywhere along the timeline.

When the rainbow lines push in toward the center, that means that either Jan or Ashleé experienced a cultural touchpoint. On the right are Ashleé’s first two touchpoints: Kelly Kapowski on Saved by the Bell and Raven Symone on The Cosby Show. Each touchpoint can be attached to multiple themes, or none at all — that’s why these touchpoints appear on Jan’s side along the black line.
When the lines with the same theme collide in the center, that’s a queernection! Here, both Jan And Ashleé felt a Girl Power connection with Lori "Ice" Fetrick on American Gladiators.

Tap any circle with a plus sign to add it to your own personal queer canon list, and tap any circle with an x to remove it. You can manage your list in the events drawer at the bottom. We’ll use this to show the all your queernections later.
